attempts.label: DANDI:000715
attempts.paper_title: NeuroPAL: A Multicolor Atlas for Whole-Brain Neuronal Identification in C. elegans
attempts.entry_title: NeuroPAL atlas and neuron identification (Yemini et al. 2021)
attempts.summary: In this head-only data, the atlas findings held but the identification results did not. Positional variability differs across neuron types, OLLR is more variable than OLLL, and NeuroPAL's color-violation figure matched. Head identification accuracy was 39 to 63% against the paper's 86%, and the eight-annotation and position-only results also failed, most likely because the five dorsal-ventral heads are stored rotated and the paper does not say how worms were oriented. Every tail result could not be tested because the dataset has no tails. The 3-reporter optimal coloring was blocked because the paper gives no sparsity. I did not create `summaries/000715-yemini-2021-01.md`.
attempts.description: Tests the atlas and identification findings of Yemini, Lin, Nejatbakhsh et al. (2021) on dandiset 000715, which holds the head volumes and hand-annotated neurons of the paper's ten NeuroPAL atlas worms. It fits the statistical atlas, tests positional variability, automatic detection, leave-one-out identification with and without color, guided annotation, calibration and the color violations of the NeuroPAL map and of the paper's optimal-coloring solutions. A notebook of its own tests some whole-brain activity findings on the paper's Zenodo record, which the dandiset does not hold.

outcomes.notes: Head atlas of 198 neurons fit on the ten heads. Among the 191 neurons named in at least eight worms the largest per-neuron positional standard deviation is 36.1, 21.2 and 13.1 times the smallest along the three principal axes of the atlas means (13.6 against 0.38 um along the major axis), and the 90th over 10th percentile ratios are 8.3, 3.2 and 3.7. Every variant of the atlas fit (two other initial worms, 5 or 100 alternations, no gauge, the forward regression of equation 4.11) gives ratios of 9.39 or more along every axis. The criterion asks for the difference within the head and within the tail; the head half holds and the tail half cannot be tested, as the dandiset holds no tails, so the claim is reproduced only in part. The first record gave reproduced for the head; the outcome was changed after the verifier's round 1.
deviations: Head only. The dandiset holds the heads of the ten worms; their tails are on the paper's Zenodo record and were not used, since the claims file assigns this claim to the dataset.

Assumption. Algorithm 4 of Methods S1 as written (equations 4.13 to 4.16) does not converge on these data, because the atlas is defined only up to an affine map and the regression of the atlas means on each worm shrinks it along its minor axes at every alternation (the extents of axes 2 and 3 fall from 22.5 and 15.6 um to 0 by 300 alternations). The atlas is kept in the frame of the initial worm (after each update it is mapped back by the affine map that best fits its means to that worm's neurons) and stopped after 20 alternations, where the position block has settled. This keeps Algorithm 4's alternation and its initialisation at one worm, and is the smallest change that gives a stable atlas; variants are shown and agree, including the forward regression of equation 4.11.

Colors are read from the volumes as Methods S1 Figure 6.2 describes (median of the z-scored image in a 1.5 x 1.5 x 0.75 um patch, CELL_ID patch_hsize [3, 3, 0]), as the files hold no per-neuron colors.

Neurons missing from a worm (the dandiset names 186 to 193 per head, against 195 in the paper) are left out of that worm's alignment and moments, and a ridge of 0.01 um^2 is added to every covariance (a standard choice) so that the 7 neurons named in fewer than 8 worms have an invertible covariance. The ridge bounds each standard deviation below by 0.1 um, which sets the smallest values of the all-neuron table; the table of neurons named in at least 8 worms, which decides the claim, is not affected.

outcomes.notes: Along the major axis of the head atlas OLLR's standard deviation is 2.69 um and OLLL's 1.25 um, ratio 2.14 (reading a, given as measured); the variance ratio is 4.60 (reading b); the extent of the 50% contour of the conditional distribution in the planes of axes 1 and 2 and of axes 1 and 3 gives 1.63 and 2.06 (reading c). Under the six variants of the atlas fit (including the forward regression of equation 4.11) the standard deviation ratio is 2.00 to 2.33 and the variance ratio 4.01 to 5.44. Both neurons are named in all ten worms.
deviations: The atlas is fit with the gauge and the 20 alternations of the assumption stated under fig2cd-variability-differs; the variants shown all give a ratio above 2 under reading b and 2.00 or more under reading a.
Which minor axis is left-right and which dorsal-ventral is not fixed by the atlas; reading c is shown in both planes.

outcomes.notes: Head only. On the named annotated neurons (reading a) Algorithm 5 as written gives 39.05, 39.04, 51.80 and 51.76% (mean per worm and pooled, per neuron and by class for left/right pairs) and the CELL_ID alignment 55.00 to 63.25%. On the automatic detections of ms1-detection-accuracy (reading b), with 82.8% of the named neurons matched to a detection, Algorithm 5 gives 21.4 to 27.6% and the CELL_ID alignment 24.8 to 30.7%. No reading of the paper's two alignments reaches 77.4%, so their outcomes agree; the atlas variants give 38.7 to 67.0% with them. The files record no orientation, and the five heads imaged in dorsal-ventral view (subject names ending DV) are stored rotated by 92.6 to 102.7 degrees about the long axis relative to the atlas (rotation part of the alignment by true correspondences), against 1.8 to 12.9 degrees for the left-right heads. Algorithm 5's identity start gives 9.6% on average on the DV heads and 68.5% on the LR heads. The CELL_ID rotation search re-runs the principal-axis fit after each rotation, as CELL_ID does, so its 52 candidates give 4 distinct starts. Started from the identity and from rotations of 90, 180 and 270 degrees about the long axis, keeping the run with the lowest assignment cost (a variant, not the paper's method), Algorithm 5 gives 74.75, 74.67, 77.38 and 77.30%, all below 77.4% (81.0% on the DV heads, 68.5% on the LR heads); the highest, 77.38% by class with the mean over worms, misses the bound by 0.02 points. Under the four atlas variants this rotated start gives 73.0 to 79.4% by class and 68.1 to 70.8% per neuron. Both class readings are inside the tolerance with 5 alternations (79.40 and 79.35%) and with the other initial worm (78.76 and 78.72%), only the mean-per-worm class reading with no gauge (77.43%, pooled 77.35%), and neither with 100 alternations; no per-neuron reading is inside under any variant. With orientation undone, which the paper's method does not do here, the outcome would turn on the atlas fit and the reading by a few hundredths of a point. Aligning each held-out worm by its true correspondences (not the paper's method) gives 77.72 to 80.22%, so even a perfect alignment of this atlas lies at the lower edge of the tolerance. Algorithm 5 converged in every worm under both starts. The tail value (94%) cannot be tested.
deviations: Head only; the tails are not in the dandiset.
The atlas fit rests on the assumption stated under fig2cd-variability-differs.

The CELL_ID variant makes the worm's principal-axis frame a proper rotation before the search, so that no candidate is a mirror image (CELL_ID rejects mirror solutions, and with an improper frame every candidate was rejected); CELL_ID's atlas is centred on its principal axes, so ours is expressed in its own principal-axis frame for this variant. Its search over theta is ported as written and has no effect (see notes).

A variant not in the paper starts Algorithm 5 from four rotations about the long axis, because the files carry no orientation and half the heads are stored in another one; it uses no annotations. It changes no outcome on the main atlas (see notes for the atlas variants).
Two named neurons of one held-out worm whose names are not in the nine-worm atlas count as wrong.
The detection behind reading b is a Python port (see ms1-detection-accuracy).

outcomes.notes: The criterion compares every tail ganglion with the head's ventral ganglion, and the dandiset holds no tails. The tail volumes of the same worms are on the paper's Zenodo record (doi:10.5281/zenodo.3906530); the claims file assigns the claim to the dataset with labels, so they were not used. It also depends on fig7bc-identification-accuracy, which was not reproduced. The head part the criterion asks to report is shown, with ganglia from the CELL_ID neuron tables (Data/NeuroPAL/herm_data.mat). The ventral ganglion has the lowest pooled accuracy of the seven head ganglia under every alignment (12.9% with Algorithm 5, 22.1% with the CELL_ID alignment, 29.3% with the rotated starts, 31.6% with the true correspondences; the other six range from 39.7 to 63.1% with Algorithm 5 and from 62.9 to 96.9% with the rotated starts). By median distance to the nearest atlas neuron (1.87 um) it is the second densest head ganglion after the dorsal ganglion (1.56 um, 6 neurons), and the third by neurons per convex-hull volume; across the seven head ganglia accuracy does not follow density (Spearman rho -0.25 to 0.04).

After eight annotations of the least certain neurons, the mean head accuracy over held-out worms is 43.0 (highest entropy, given as measured) and 43.1% (lowest top probability) with Algorithm 5, from 39.1%, and 58.8 and 58.7% with the CELL_ID alignment, from 55.0%; over the unannotated neurons only 40.5 to 57.0%. No held-out worm exceeds 90% with these alignments (the best worm reaches 83.0% with Algorithm 5 and 86.2 to 86.7% with the CELL_ID alignment). With the rotated starts of fig7bc-identification-accuracy (not the paper's method) it is 79.3 and 78.4%, from 74.8%, with one worm above 90% (91.5%, entropy ranking).
deviations: Runs on the leave-one-out identifications of fig7bc-identification-accuracy, and so rests on the same atlas assumption.

outcomes.notes: Head only. With the most uncertain neurons annotated first, the mean accuracy over worms is above the mean of 100 random orders at all 50 annotation counts, under both rankings and all three alignments, and its mean over 1 to 50 annotations is higher (68.0 against 62.4% with the CELL_ID alignment and entropy ranking, 52.2 against 48.5% with Algorithm 5, 86.8 against 79.0% with the rotated starts). At 50 annotations it is 79.1 against 69.5% with the CELL_ID alignment; at 8, 58.8 against 57.3% (43.0 against 42.1% with Algorithm 5, 79.3 against 76.0% with the rotated starts). The criterion asks for this in head and tail; the head half holds and the tail half cannot be tested, so the claim is reproduced only in part. The statement's "much faster" is a gap of 3.5 to 7.8 points between the means over the range and 1 to 3 points at eight annotations. The first record gave reproduced for the head; the outcome was changed after the verifier's round 1.
deviations: Head only; the tails are not in the dandiset.
Rests on the identifications of fig7bc-identification-accuracy and its atlas assumption.

outcomes.notes: Head only. With positions alone, accuracy is 20.4 to 22.8% with Algorithm 5 and 24.3 to 27.1% with the CELL_ID alignment over the four readings, below 45%; under every reading it is below the full model, as the claim says. With the rotated starts of fig7bc-identification-accuracy, which undo the orientation of the dorsal-ventral heads (not the paper's method), it is 43.1 to 44.0%, still below 45%; under the atlas variants the rotated starts give 45.1 to 46.7% with 5 alternations, the other initial worm and no gauge, inside the tolerance, and 37.8 to 38.8% with 100 alternations. Aligning by the true correspondences (not the paper's method either) gives 48.7 to 49.4%, inside 45 to 55%. The tail value cannot be tested.
deviations: Head only; the tails are not in the dandiset.
Same atlas assumption as fig2cd-variability-differs, applied to a position-only atlas.

outcomes.notes: Head only, K = 191 on each of the ten heads, against all 189 to 196 stored neurons. Mean accuracy 71.0% (SD 4.6, per head 64.4 to 80.3%), just below 72 to 88%; mean precision 83.4% and recall 82.5%, inside 81 to 99%. Against the named neurons only, 70.6, 82.5 and 82.8%. SLSQP reported success in 2,043 of the 2,064 Gaussian fits in this run. Whether MATLAB's fmincon would place the detections differently, which could move the accuracy across its bound, is not measured; scipy's trust-constr optimiser was tried while preparing and was too slow for the notebook, so it is not run here. The tail values cannot be tested.
deviations: Head only; the tails are not in the dandiset.

The detection is a Python port of CELL_ID (Preprocess.filter_gut_lysosomes, AutoDetect.detect and fit_gaussian) with its default parameters (minimum eigenvalue 0.1, exclusion radius 1.5 um, eigenvalue bounds 0.01 to 5, detection at 0.4 um). fmincon (interior point) is replaced by scipy's SLSQP with the same bounds and constraints, MATLAB's imresize3 by scikit-image's resize with antialiasing, and the in-plane Gaussian blur of imgaussfilt by scipy's filter. Any of these can shift detections.
Whether the paper's hand annotations include the stored neurons that have no name is not said; both are shown.

outcomes.notes: The criterion's two readings disagree, which it says blocks the claim. Reading a holds in every run (Spearman rho 0.51 to 0.70 between per-neuron confidence and accuracy, p 2.1e-14 or lower, 198 neurons); reading b fails in every run (confidence averages 87.1 to 89.4% and accuracy 37.9 to 61.8%, a mean absolute difference of 27.8 to 49.2 points against a bound of 10). With the rotated starts of fig7bc-identification-accuracy (not the paper's method) rho is 0.81 to 0.82 and the difference 16.3 to 17.7 points, so the readings still disagree. The overconfidence follows from the low identification accuracy of fig7bc-identification-accuracy. The paper gives no measure of agreement; the question is recorded as a finding for its authors. Head only.

With neighbors from the dandiset's head atlas (192 neurons with a NeuroPAL color, 4065 adjacent ordered pairs), the code's measure, the mean shortfall below the margin over neighboring pairs, is 3.64%, inside 3.5 +/- 0.35, and 3.62 to 3.66% under the atlas variants. The paper's own inputs in data.mat give 3.47% (this port of computeProbAdjacency agrees with data.mat's adjacency on 98.9% of entries). The Methods share of neighboring pairs closer in color than 1/3, now a variant, is 21.50% on the head atlas and on data.mat alike. What the answer changed. The first run tested the claims file's earlier criterion, which took the Methods share as the main result, and recorded not_reproduced (21.50%) with a question to a reader. The reader amended the claim (questions/000715.yaml), so that the code's mean shortfall decides it and the share is a variant, and the statement now reads "theoretical color margin violation of 3.5%". Under the amended claim the same numbers give reproduced. Pooled head and tail cannot be tested; the head-only reading is one the criterion names.
deviations: Head atlas only; the tails are not in the dandiset.
Six atlas neurons (AMSOL, AMSOR, DA2, DB3, HMC, VD3) have no NeuroPAL color in data.mat and are left out.
The random samples of computeProbAdjacency use numpy with seed 1, not MATLAB's rng(1).

outcomes.notes: On the neighbors of ms2-neuropal-color-violations (dandiset head atlas, 192 neurons, 543 Brain Atlas reporters with distinct patterns over them), the best of 10,000 runs at sparsity 100 has a mean shortfall of 1.71 to 1.72% (27 to 30 reporters kept), inside 1.7 +/- 0.17; the best run keeping exactly 39 reporters (189 to 205 runs) has 1.83 to 1.86%, also inside. These values differ in the second decimal between machines with the same seeds; the ranges are those of the runs made for this attempt. The sparsity for 3 reporters is not given, and the criterion's reading, the sparsity whose solutions use 3 reporters, fits 1500, 2000 and 3000 of the scan, where most runs keep 3 reporters (95, 94 and 89 of 100). With the criterion's 7,500 runs the best 3-reporter value is 6.95% at 1500 (7,106 runs with 3 reporters) and 8.38% at 2000 (7,020 runs), below 9.45 to 11.55, and 9.90% at 3000 (6,253 runs, none below 9.45%), inside it (optimal_coloring_sparsity.ipynb); at 1000 the best of 1,000 runs (561 with 3 reporters) is 7.83%. The 39-reporter value is inside the tolerance under every reading. The outcome would be partially reproduced at 1500 and 2000 and reproduced at 3000, and no sparsity is better supported than the others, so the claim is blocked with every result shown, by the rule this attempt applies to fig6de-asj-ric-stimulus-specific. The first record gave partially reproduced at 1500; the change was proposed after round 2 and agreed in round 3. The 3-reporter solutions take few values (5th percentile 9.90% at 1500), so the best of fewer runs lands in the tolerance, in 95% of random subsets of 10 runs, 66% of 100 and 1% of 1,000. On the paper's own adjacency in data.mat (235 neurons, 654 unique reporters as the paper states, 1,000 runs each) the best is 1.74 to 1.81% at sparsity 100 (1.99 to 2.03% for exactly 39 reporters) and 8.71% for 3 reporters. The Methods share, a variant, is 13.65% and 20.84% for the two best head-atlas solutions. What the answer changed. The amended criterion takes the code's mean shortfall as the measure, in place of the Methods share. The first run had blocked this claim (not_runnable) because scipy cannot read the MATLAB table holding the reporters; the author-answers run read it with mat-io and ported the solver. A question is recorded for a reader on whether the 3-reporter value is the best of 7,500 runs of this one setting, as the criterion reads it, or of the part of the paper's 7,500 simulations that had this setting (Methods S2 Figure 1 and Figure 6 legends), since with fewer runs the best falls in the tolerance.
deviations: Head atlas only (192 neurons); the paper used 235 head and tail neurons. The paper's own adjacency is run as a reference with 1,000 runs per setting, not 10,000 and 7,500.

optimal_color_solver.m ported to Python and run on many random starts at once; starts are drawn with numpy, not MATLAB's rand, and the loop over neighbors uses squared distances over the nonzero entries of A, which gives the code's updates up to rounding.

Three intensities taken as the margin of 1/3, from Methods S2 section 4.2 ("1/3 as our minimum color margin (corresponding to discriminating 3 levels of color intensity)"); 300 iterations from optimal_color_parameters.m and Methods S2 section 4.2 ("300 iterations in total").

The solution kept from a set of runs is the one with the fewest violations, from the Methods S2 Figure 1 legend ("chosen as those with the minimal color violations, among 10,000 simulations"); each solution's colors and kept reporters follow find_optimal_colors.m (Otsu threshold on X, colors scaled by each channel's maximum).

The sparsity for 3 reporters is not given by the paper; it was chosen as the value of a scan (250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000; 100 runs each) whose runs most often keep 3 reporters, as the criterion reads it. Sparsities 2000 and 3000 were also run with 7,500 runs each, and 1000 with 1,000 runs, in optimal_coloring_sparsity.ipynb, a notebook of its own to keep each within its time limit.

On the Zenodo record (21 OH16230 heads, histogram-normalised traces), ASEL's mean change from the 10 s before NaCl to the 10 s of NaCl is 1.01 and ASER's 0.42; the two-tailed unpaired t test gives t = 3.82, p = 0.00046 (21 against 21). ASER rises in 14 of 21 worms (one-sample p = 0.0032). With similar neurons removed (both members) p = 0.0019 (17 against 17) and ASER rises by 0.46; with one member removed the numbers are those without removal.
deviations: The response is the mean during the stimulus minus the mean of the identical period before it, as the STAR Methods define a response; the asymmetry test is applied to these changes.

outcomes.notes: The criterion says only that the claim is not tested on the dandiset and gives no test for "stochastically asymmetric" responses; with the run's time spent on the dandiset's claims no criterion was derived from the paper. The data are on the Zenodo record (is_AWCL_OFF gives the ON/OFF assignment per worm).

AIN, AVF, AVH, AVJ, I2 and MI all respond to NaCl with q of at most 0.05 (paired two-tailed t test of the stimulus against the period before, Storey q-values over the tested neurons) under the three readings of the removal of similar neurons; the largest q is 0.041 (AVF, no removal) and 0.039 (AVJ, both members removed). All six rise. Storey's pi0 for the head's NaCl tests is 0.45 to 0.47 at lambda = 0.5; the bootstrap choice of lambda over 0.01 to 0.95 (Storey 2002, the default of MATLAB's mafdr) gives pi0 of 0.40 to 0.43 and a largest q of 0.033 to 0.038, so the outcome holds under both estimates. With pi0 = 1, the Benjamini-Hochberg bound and not Storey's method, AVF and AVJ have q of 0.062 to 0.088 under every reading.
deviations: Storey's pi0 is estimated at lambda = 0.5, a standard choice the paper does not give; the bootstrap choice of lambda (MATLAB mafdr's default) and pi0 = 1 are shown.

outcomes.notes: The claims file gives no criterion ("Not tested on the dandiset") and the paper gives no measure of "more inhibitory activity"; not attempted within the run's time. The data are on the Zenodo record.

The outcome depends on whether both members of a pair of similar neurons (within 5 um, traces correlated at 0.95 or more) were removed, which the paper does not say. Without removal, and with one member removed, both statements hold. ASJ is excited by NaCl (q 0.0013 and 0.0017) and inhibited by 2-butanone (q 0.0009 and 0.0014) and 2,3-pentanedione (q 0.019 and 0.033); RIC is excited by 2,3-pentanedione (q 0.0044 and 0.019) and not by NaCl (q 0.065 and 0.054) or 2-butanone. With both members removed, ASJ's fall with 2,3-pentanedione is not significant (mean change -0.091, q 0.063) and RIC also responds to NaCl (q 0.044). Removing both drops 647 of 3,550 head traces, removing one 353. The responding sets overlap and differ under every reading (9 or 10 of 60 to 65 responding neurons respond to all three stimuli). With the bootstrap choice of Storey's lambda the pattern is the same (RIC to NaCl q 0.060 without removal and 0.049 with one member removed; with both removed ASJ to 2,3-pentanedione q 0.055 and RIC to NaCl q 0.037). The first record took removal of both members as an assumption and gave not_reproduced; after the verifier's round 1 no reading is held to be better supported than the others, so the claim is blocked with the result of every reading shown. The question is recorded as a finding for the paper's authors.
deviations: The STAR Methods remove neurons within 5 um whose traces correlate at 0.95 or more ("were deemed too similar and removed") without saying whether both members of a pair go; the record's README says they are kept in the files. All three readings are run. The correlation is taken on the dF/F0 traces.
Storey's pi0 at lambda = 0.5, a standard choice; the bootstrap choice of lambda and pi0 = 1 are shown.

outcomes.notes: The outcome depends on the removal of similar neurons, which the paper leaves open. On the 21 tails, PVQ is excited by 2,3-pentanedione under every reading (mean change 0.048 to 0.049, q 0.0006 to 0.0008) and by neither other stimulus. Post-stimulus responders exist for all three stimuli without removal (NaCl LUA, PHB, PVW; 2-butanone LUA, PHA, PHB, PVR; 2,3-pentanedione eleven neurons) and with one member removed (NaCl LUA only), but with both members removed none remains for NaCl. So the claim holds in full on the criterion under two of the three readings and in part under the third, and by the rule the notebook states and applies to fig6de-asj-ric-stimulus-specific it is blocked with every result shown. The first record gave partially reproduced, the outcome every reading supports; the change was proposed after round 2 and agreed in round 3. Removing both drops 161 of 797 tail traces. With the bootstrap choice of Storey's lambda the pattern is the same (no NaCl responder with both members removed), though the bootstrap gives pi0 = 0 for some of the tail's small sets of tests. Which responders are sensory and which interneurons was not tested, as neither the record nor the claims file gives neuron types.
deviations: Same open detail on the removal of similar neurons as fig6de-asj-ric-stimulus-specific; all three readings are run.
The post-stimulus window is the 10 s after the stimulus, the stimulus length; the paper does not give it.

Over 31 AVF traces from 18 heads, the median rate of peaks in traces median filtered at 0.5 s is 0.197, 0.109 and 0.071 per second at prominences of 0.5, 1 and 1.5 standard deviations (the first given as measured), and the median frequency of the largest spectral power is 0.19 Hz; 1 (peak count) and 3 (spectrum) of 31 traces fall in 0.27 to 0.33 Hz. The 0.5 s median filter is 2 samples at 4 Hz; the median filter needs an odd window, so 3 samples (0.75 s) are used. All 31 AVF traces from 18 worms are pooled, as the five worms of Figure S1H are not named.

findings.statement: Every file gives strain OH16230 (the NeuroPAL;GCaMP6s strain of the whole-brain recordings), a spinning disk confocal, a worm "in microfluidic chip", birth on 2021-01-05 and imaging on 2021-01-07. The files are the heads of the paper's ten otIs669 (OH15262) atlas worms imaged on a Zeiss LSM 880; the volumes of 7_YAaLR and 76_YAaDV are identical, voxel for voxel, to the Zenodo volumes of those otIs669 worms, and the ten identifiers match.

The third channel is labelled GFP-GCaMP, with GFP emission settings, but its mean is 17,000 to 21,000 in every file, far above the fluorescence channels, and the Zenodo copies mark that channel as the DIC (transmitted light) channel. The worms carry no GCaMP.

The dandiset holds only the heads. The tails of the same ten worms, used for the paper's tail atlas and tail accuracies, are on the paper's Zenodo record, and so is the whole-brain activity of Figure 6. Nine of the claims tested here need the tails in part or in full.

The files carry no per-neuron colors (the Zenodo files have a color readout per neuron), no orientation of the worm, and do not say whether the stored voxel indices are 0- or 1-based. The five heads imaged in dorsal-ventral view are stored rotated by about 90 degrees about the long axis relative to the five imaged in left-right view, which only the subject names (ending DV or LR) hint at. Comparison with the Zenodo annotations shows that each stored voxel is the Zenodo position made 0-based and rounded. Colors had to be recomputed from the volumes.
0 to 6 of the 189 to 196 stored neurons per file have an empty name, with no description of what they are; the paper reports 195 annotated head neurons per worm.
Neuron names are stored as a ragged array of single characters (ID_labels with ID_labels_index), so each name must be joined from its characters.
The dandiset metadata name no related publication (relatedResource is empty); the description and the files' related_publications give the paper's title only, without a DOI.

Question for the paper's authors. Algorithm 4 of Methods S1 as written does not converge on these data, because the regression of the atlas means on each worm shrinks the atlas along its minor axes at every alternation. How was the atlas kept from shrinking, and after how many alternations was it stopped? This attempt kept it in the initial worm's frame and stopped after 20 alternations.

Question for the paper's authors. Algorithm 5 starts the alignment of a held-out worm at the identity, which fails on worms stored in another orientation (5 to 12% accuracy on the five dorsal-ventral heads against an atlas in a left-right worm's frame). How were held-out worms oriented before identification in the cross-validation of Figure 7B-C? Starting from four rotations about the long axis gives 75 to 77% here.

CELL_ID AutoId.local_alignment (d9f5df9) rotates each candidate by theta about the major axis and then runs the principal-axis alignment again, which undoes the rotation, so its search over 26 angles and 2 signs yields 4 distinct starts on the worm checked. The search does not explore rotations about the major axis as the code's loop suggests.

Methods S2 section 4.3 defines the color violation percentage as the share of neighboring pairs below the discrimination margin, but the reported 3.5% for NeuroPAL is the mean shortfall below the margin computed by find_optimal_colors.m. On the paper's own data.mat the share is 21.5% and the mean shortfall 3.47%.

Question for the paper's authors. Which sparsity, and how many runs of the 3-color, 3-intensity, 3-reporter setting, gave the 10.5% solution of Figure 7E and Methods S2 Figure 1? The 7,500 simulations of Methods S2 Figure 6 span 2 to 6 colors, 1 to 3 intensities and 2 to 71 reporters. A Python port of the code finds 6.95% as the best of 7,500 runs of that setting on the dandiset's head atlas at sparsity 1500, 8.38% at 2000 and 9.90% at 3000, and values within 10% of 10.5% as the best of 10 to 100 runs at 1500.

Question for the paper's authors. Methods S1 section 6.4 says confidence and accuracy are "largely in good agreement" without a measure. Which measure of agreement was meant, and which left/right pairs were scored by class under footnote 1?

Question for the paper's authors, on the Zenodo activity data. When neurons within 5 um had traces correlated at 0.95 or more, were both removed or one, and on which traces? Which window defines the post-stimulus period, which five worms and which peak rule underlie Figure S1H? The outcomes of two claims depend on the first point.

entries.name: 000715-yemini-2021
entries.title: NeuroPAL atlas and neuron identification (Yemini et al. 2021)
entries.description: Tests the atlas and identification findings of Yemini, Lin, Nejatbakhsh et al. (2021) on dandiset 000715, which holds the head volumes and hand-annotated neurons of the paper's ten NeuroPAL atlas worms. It fits the statistical atlas, tests positional variability, automatic detection, leave-one-out identification with and without color, guided annotation, calibration and the color violations of the NeuroPAL map and of the paper's optimal-coloring solutions. A notebook of its own tests some whole-brain activity findings on the paper's Zenodo record, which the dandiset does not hold.
